question: What exactly is a chemical hazard?

options.A: Only industrial gases released into the atmosphere
options.B: Biological agents that cause infectious diseases
options.C: Prescription medications administered strictly by a physician
options.D: Any chemical that can cause harm to health or the environment

explanation: You've got this! A chemical hazard is simply any substance or mixture that has the potential to cause harm to people, property, or our environment. Think of everyday harsh cleaners or lab chemicals. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h1)

question: Which of these is a common chemical hazard you would actually find inside a modern hospital?
explanation: Great job! Hospitals handle unique chemical risks every day, such as strong sterilizing liquids, anesthetic gases, and potent cancer-fighting drugs like cytotoxic agents. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h1)

question: How do corrosive chemical substances mainly damage human tissue?

options.A: By triggering sudden allergic respiratory attacks
options.B: By altering genetic DNA over many decades
options.C: By depressing the central nervous system through inhalation
options.D: By destroying living tissue upon direct physical contact

explanation: Think of strong acids or bases—when they touch your skin or mucous membranes, they cause immediate, visible chemical damage right on the spot! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h2)

question: Which chemical group includes volatile liquids like acetone that can affect your nervous system when breathed in?
explanation: Solvents evaporate easily into the air. When we breathe them in, they can travel through our system and sometimes affect our neurological function. Good to know for safe lab practices! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h2)

question: What is the main way airborne chemical vapors and dust particles quickly enter the bloodstream?
explanation: Our lungs have a huge surface area and a rich network of tiny blood vessels, making breathing in dusts or gases the fastest route right into our general circulation. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h3)

question: In the toxicokinetic process known as ADME, what does the letter 'M' stand for?
explanation: You're doing great! ADME stands for Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion. It simply describes the journey a chemical takes inside the human body. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h3)

question: Which part of the cell is usually targeted by poisons that block energy and ATP production?
explanation: Spot on! Mitochondria are the powerhouses of our cells, making ATP energy. Many metabolic poisons specifically attack and disrupt them. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h4)

question: How do free radicals and reactive oxygen species primarily damage our cells?

options.A: By stimulating excessive and uncontrollable cellular reproduction
options.B: By instantly freezing intracellular fluid and stopping circulation
options.C: By creating oxidative stress that harms DNA and cell membranes
options.D: By completely blocking the intake of dietary proteins

explanation: Free radicals love to steal electrons from nearby molecules. This creates oxidative stress, which can rough up essential parts of the cell like our DNA and protective membranes. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h4)

question: Which physical sign is a classic giveaway of an opioid overdose?
explanation: Opioids slow down the central nervous system. A classic clinical sign you'll learn to spot is profound sleepiness along with very tiny, constricted 'pinpoint' pupils. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h5)

question: A farm worker comes in with excessive drooling, tearing, sweating, and diarrhea after spraying crops. What type of poisoning is most likely?
explanation: Fantastic clinical deduction! Organophosphate pesticides cause over-stimulation of the parasympathetic system—remember the helpful SLUDGE mnemonic for all those wet secretions! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h5)

question: What is the absolute first thing a nurse should do for a patient who has a hazardous liquid chemical spilled on their skin?

options.A: Apply neutralizing acidic or basic ointments
options.D: Draw baseline arterial blood gas samples

explanation: Safety first! Stripping away the wet clothing stops the chemical from continuing to soak into the skin or burn the patient. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h6)

question: Why is it a big mistake to force a patient to vomit after swallowing a corrosive chemical?

options.A: It forces the chemical to pass too quickly into the bloodstream
options.B: It neutralizes any antidote that medical staff plan to give later
options.C: It causes severe secondary chemical burns to the esophagus
options.D: It stops the liver from metabolizing the ingested poison

explanation: Bringing a corrosive chemical back up means it burns the delicate food pipe (esophagus) and throat a second time on the way out. Never induce vomiting for corrosives! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h6)

question: Which medication is the standard, go-to antidote for a paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose?
explanation: You'll see this often in practice! Acetylcysteine saves the liver by restocking glutathione, which neutralizes the toxic breakdown products of paracetamol. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h7)

question: How does naloxone work to reverse an opioid overdose?

options.A: By speeding up renal excretion of the drug through urination
options.B: By binding directly to the free poison molecules in the stomach
options.C: By competing for and blocking opioid receptor sites
options.D: By stimulating the liver to break down the circulating toxin

explanation: Naloxone acts like a key that bumps the opioid off its lock (the receptor). By blocking those sites, it quickly wakes the patient up and helps them breathe again. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h7)

question: Where can healthcare workers quickly find safety details, hazard warnings, and emergency steps for a specific chemical?
explanation: Every hospital department has them. The Safety Data Sheet (SDS) is your best friend for looking up how to safely handle a chemical and what to do if an accident happens. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h8)

question: Which practice is strictly forbidden when handling chemicals in any hospital or lab setting?

options.A: Reading the manufacturer safety sheet before opening the package
options.B: Reporting minor chemical spill near-misses to safety officers
options.C: Transferring chemicals into unlabeled food or drink containers
options.D: Wearing protective gloves and face shields during dilution

explanation: Never put chemicals in old juice or water bottles! Someone could easily mistake it for a drink and suffer accidental poisoning. Always keep containers properly labeled. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h8)
